title: Shell basics and getting help
objective: Access shell prompts, issue commands with correct syntax, and find answers in man, info and /usr/share/doc.

questions.q: In the prompt `[student@servera ~]$`, what does the final `$` tell you?
options: You are logged in as a regular (non-root) user
You are logged in as root
A command is still running in the background
questions.explain: A `$` prompt means a normal user; `#` means root. Always glance at it before running admin commands.

questions.q: Which command searches the short descriptions of all man pages for a keyword?
questions.explain: `man -k` is the same as `apropos`. If it returns "nothing appropriate", build the index as root with `mandb`.

questions.q: Which man section documents configuration file formats such as /etc/fstab?
questions.explain: Section 1 = user commands, 5 = file formats, 8 = admin commands. Use `man 5 fstab`.

questions.q: Open the manual page for the /etc/passwd file format (not the passwd command).
questions.explain: Without the section number, `man passwd` opens section 1, the command.

questions.q: Where do packages usually install extra documentation such as example config files?
questions.explain: Look in `/usr/share/doc/<package>` for READMEs and examples. It is available during the exam.

questions.q: Which keyboard shortcut searches backwards through your bash command history?
questions.explain: Press Ctrl+R, type part of an old command, press Ctrl+R again to go further back, Enter to run it.

questions.q: Show only the last 20 commands from your history.
questions.explain: `history` alone shows everything; `!N` reruns entry number N.

questions.q: What does `!!` do in bash?
options: Repeats the last argument of the previous command
Inverts the exit code of the last command
Opens the history file in an editor
questions.explain: `!!` is the whole last command (handy as `sudo !!`). `!$` is only the last argument.

questions.q: Find out whether `cd` is a shell builtin, an alias, or a program on disk.
questions.explain: `type` reports how bash resolves a name. Builtins have no separate man page; use `help cd`.

questions.q: Inside a man page, how do you search forward for the word "UID"?
options: Type /UID and press Enter, then n for the next match
questions.explain: man uses the `less` pager: `/pattern` searches forward, `n` next match, `N` previous, `q` quit.

labs.title: Find answers only with the built-in documentation
labs.scenario: Without using the internet, find out: (1) which man section documents /etc/shadow, (2) which useradd option sets a specific UID, and (3) which commands have "partition" in their description.
hints: `man -f name` lists every section that has a page with that name.
If `man -k` finds nothing, the index has not been built yet.
steps: man useradd        # then type /UID and press n
sudo mandb         # only if man -k printed "nothing appropriate"

labs.title: Practise history and shell shortcuts
labs.scenario: Run five different commands. Rerun the third one by its history number, reuse the last argument of a command with `!$`, find an old command with Ctrl+R, then save your whole history to ~/myhistory.txt.

title: Managing files and directories
objective: Create, delete, copy and move files and directories; understand the filesystem hierarchy.

questions.q: Where are system-wide configuration files kept on RHEL?
questions.explain: `/etc` holds configuration. `/usr` holds installed software, `/var` holds variable data such as logs.

questions.q: Which directory holds data that changes while the system runs, such as logs, spools and caches?
questions.explain: Logs live in `/var/log`, for example `/var/log/messages` and `/var/log/secure`.

questions.q: Which of these paths is absolute?
questions.explain: An absolute path starts with `/` and works from any current directory.

questions.q: Create the directory tree a/b/c in one command, creating missing parents.
questions.explain: Without `-p`, mkdir fails if `a` or `a/b` doesn't exist.

questions.q: Copy the directory /etc/skel and everything inside it to /tmp/skelcopy.
questions.explain: Directories need `-r`. `-a` (archive) also keeps permissions, ownership and timestamps.

questions.q: What is the difference between `rmdir dir` and `rm -r dir`?
options: rmdir only removes empty directories; rm -r removes the directory and its contents
rmdir asks for confirmation; rm -r never deletes hidden files
questions.explain: Use `rmdir` when you want a safety check that a directory is empty.

questions.q: Which files does the glob `file?.txt` match?
options: file1.txt and fileA.txt, but not file10.txt
Only a file literally named file?.txt
questions.explain: `?` matches exactly one character, `*` matches any number, `[abc]` matches one of a set.

questions.q: Create report1.txt through report5.txt with a single touch command.
questions.explain: Brace expansion `{1..5}` expands to 1 2 3 4 5 before the command runs.

questions.q: As a regular user with no aliases, what happens with `mv a.txt b.txt` when b.txt already exists?
options: b.txt is overwritten without any prompt
mv refuses and prints an error
questions.explain: Use `mv -i` to be asked first. On RHEL, root has aliases `rm -i`, `cp -i` and `mv -i` set in /root/.bashrc.

questions.q: Go back to the directory you were in just before the current one.
questions.explain: `cd -` toggles between your last two directories. `cd` alone goes home.

labs.title: File management workout
labs.scenario: As student, build ~/lab2 with subdirectories projects, archive and trash. Create notes1.txt to notes3.txt inside projects. Copy notes1.txt into archive, rename notes2.txt to draft.txt, move notes3.txt into trash, then delete the trash directory with everything in it.
hints: Brace expansion saves typing for both mkdir and touch.

labs.title: Tour the filesystem hierarchy
labs.scenario: Find where these live on your RHEL VM and note them down: the SSH server config file, the kernel image, the `ls` binary, the system log file, and the home directory of root.

title: Links and finding files
objective: Create hard and soft links, and locate files with find.

questions.q: What is true about a hard link?
options: It points to the same inode as the original file
It stores the path of the original file
It breaks when the original file is deleted
It can point to a directory
questions.explain: Hard links are extra names for the same inode. The data stays until the last name is removed.

questions.q: What happens to a symbolic link when its target file is deleted?
options: The link remains but is broken (dangling)
The link keeps a copy of the data
questions.explain: A soft link stores a path. If nothing exists at that path, the link is broken. `ls -l` shows it in red.

questions.q: Which of these can a hard link NOT do?
options: Point to a directory or to a file on another filesystem
Point to a file in the same directory
Share the same inode as the original
questions.explain: Soft links can cross filesystems and point to directories; hard links cannot.

questions.q: Create a symbolic link /root/hosts-link that points to /etc/hosts.
questions.explain: Order: `ln -s TARGET LINKNAME`. Leave out `-s` to make a hard link.

questions.q: Find every file on the system owned by user natasha, hiding "Permission denied" errors.
questions.explain: `2>/dev/null` discards error messages from directories you cannot read.

questions.q: Which find test matches files larger than 100 MiB?
questions.explain: `+` means more than, `-` means less than. Units: k, M, G.

questions.q: Find files under /etc that were modified in the last 2 days.
questions.explain: `-mtime -2` = less than 2 days ago. Use `-mmin` for minutes.

questions.q: In `find / -user harry -exec cp -a {} /root/harry/ \;` what does `{}` stand for?
questions.explain: `\;` ends the -exec command. find runs it once for every match, putting the path in place of `{}`.

questions.q: What does the second column of `ls -l` output show for a file?
options: The number of hard links to it
The number of users who opened it
questions.explain: `ls -i` shows the inode number. A link count of 2 on a file means one extra hard link exists.

questions.q: Find every file under /usr that has the SUID bit set.
questions.explain: `-perm -4000` means "at least these bits". `ls -l` shows SUID as an `s` in the owner execute slot.

labs.title: Hard links vs soft links
labs.scenario: In ~/linklab create original.txt containing "version 1". Make a hard link hard.txt and a soft link soft.txt. Compare inode numbers, delete original.txt, and see which link still shows the content.
steps: cat soft.txt       # No such file or directory

labs.title: Find a user's files and copy them (exam classic)
labs.scenario: Create user harry and give him a few files in /tmp and his home. Then, as root, find every regular file owned by harry and copy it into /root/harryfiles, keeping permissions.
hints: Create the destination directory before running find.

title: Redirection and pipes
objective: Use input-output redirection (>, >>,

questions.q: What does `2>` redirect?
questions.explain: File descriptors: 0 = stdin, 1 = stdout, 2 = stderr.

questions.q: What does `command > out.txt 2>&1` do?
options: Sends both standard output and standard error to out.txt
Sends output to out.txt and errors to a file called 1
questions.explain: `2>&1` means "send stderr to wherever stdout goes now". The order matters.

questions.q: With `command 2>&1 > file`, where do the errors go?
options: Nowhere; bash reports a syntax error
questions.explain: Redirections are processed left to right. At the time of `2>&1`, stdout still pointed at the terminal.

questions.q: Append the line "hello" to notes.txt without overwriting it.
questions.explain: `>` truncates the file first. `>>` appends.

questions.q: Search the whole filesystem for files named passwd, throwing away all error messages.
questions.explain: /dev/null discards everything written to it.

questions.q: What does `tee` do?
options: Copies its input to a file and to standard output at the same time
Splits a file into two parts
Joins two files side by side
questions.explain: Example: `ls -l | tee list.txt | wc -l` saves the listing and still counts it.

questions.q: Save the output of `ls -l /etc` to /root/etc.txt and also show it on the screen.
questions.explain: Use `tee -a` to append instead of overwrite.

questions.q: In bash, what does `&> file` do?
options: Redirects both stdout and stderr to file
Runs the command in the background and writes to file
questions.explain: `&> file` is short for `> file 2>&1`. Use `&>> file` to append both.

questions.q: What does the pipe `|` connect?
options: The stdout of the left command to the stdin of the right command
The stderr of the left command to the right command
The exit code of the left command to the right command
questions.explain: Errors are not piped unless you add `2>&1` first (or use `|&`).

questions.q: Count the number of lines in /etc/passwd.
questions.explain: Each line in /etc/passwd is one account, so this also counts accounts.

labs.title: Redirection practice
labs.scenario: Run `ls /etc /nonexistent` four ways: output only to ok.txt, errors only to err.txt, both to all.txt, and append a second run to all.txt. Check each file after every step.

labs.title: Build a pipeline
labs.scenario: Show the 5 largest files in /usr/bin with their sizes in human-readable form and save that list to /root/biggest.txt while also printing it.
steps: # head -n 6 because the first line of ls -l is the "total" line

title: Editing and viewing text files
objective: Create and edit text files with vim; read files with cat, less, head and tail.

questions.q: In vim, how do you save the file and quit?
options: Press Esc, then type :wq and Enter
questions.explain: `:wq` writes and quits. `:x` or `ZZ` do the same but only write if the file changed.

questions.q: In vim, how do you quit without saving your changes?
questions.explain: The `!` forces vim to discard changes.

questions.q: In vim normal (command) mode, what does `dd` do?
questions.explain: `yy` copies a line, `p` pastes below, `u` undoes, `Ctrl+R` redoes.

questions.q: Which vim keys jump to the last line and to the first line of the file?
options: G for the last line, gg for the first
:$ for the first line, :0 for the last
questions.explain: `:25` or `25G` jumps to line 25. `:set nu` shows line numbers.

questions.q: How do you replace every "foo" with "bar" in the whole file in vim?
questions.explain: `%` means every line, `g` means every match on each line. Add `c` to confirm each one.

questions.q: Show only the first 5 lines of /etc/passwd.
questions.explain: `tail -n 5` shows the last 5 lines.

questions.q: Watch /var/log/messages live as new lines are written to it.
questions.explain: Stop following with Ctrl+C. `journalctl -f` does the same for the journal.

questions.q: Which command opens an interactive vim lesson you can practise on?
questions.explain: Doing `vimtutor` once takes about 30 minutes and covers everything needed for the exam.

questions.q: Open /etc/services one screen at a time so you can scroll up and down and search.
questions.explain: In `less`: Space = next page, b = back, /word = search, q = quit.

questions.q: In vim, which key enters insert mode before the cursor, and which opens a new line below?
options: i inserts before the cursor; o opens a new line below
a inserts before the cursor; O opens a line below
I inserts at the cursor; n opens a line below
Insert key only; there is no key for a new line
questions.explain: `a` appends after the cursor, `A` at the end of the line, `O` opens a line above.

labs.title: vim speed drill
labs.scenario: Copy /etc/services to ~/services.txt and open it in vim. Show line numbers, jump to line 100, delete 3 lines, go to the end of the file, add a line "# edited by me", replace every "tcp" with "TCP", then save and quit.
steps: # :set nu   ->  :100  ->  3dd  ->  G  ->  o  type the text  ->  Esc

labs.title: Read logs efficiently
labs.scenario: As root, show the first 10 and last 10 lines of /var/log/secure, open it in less and search for "session opened", then follow it live while you log in from a second terminal.
steps: tail -f /var/log/secure   # in another terminal: ssh student@localhost

title: grep and regular expressions
objective: Use grep and regular expressions to analyze text.

questions.q: Show the lines of /etc/passwd that start with "root".
questions.explain: `^` anchors the match to the start of the line.

questions.q: Which regular expression matches lines that end with "bash"?
questions.explain: `$` anchors to the end of the line. `^$` matches an empty line.

questions.q: In a basic regular expression, what does `.` match?
questions.explain: Escape it as `\.` to match a real dot, for example `grep '\.conf$'`.

questions.q: Show all lines in /etc/ssh/sshd_config that are neither comments nor empty lines.
questions.explain: This is the quickest way to see what a config file really sets.

questions.q: What does `grep -E 'cat|dog' file` print?
options: Lines containing cat followed by dog
Only the words cat and dog
questions.explain: `-E` turns on extended regex so `|`, `+`, `?` and `{n}` work without backslashes.

questions.q: Count how many lines in /etc/passwd contain "nologin".
questions.explain: `-c` prints a count instead of the lines.

questions.q: What does `grep -w root` do differently from `grep root`?
options: It only matches "root" as a whole word
questions.explain: With `-w`, "rootkit" and "chroot" no longer match.

questions.q: Search every file under /etc for "PermitRootLogin" and show file names with line numbers.
questions.explain: `-r` recursive, `-n` line numbers, `-i` ignore case, `-l` file names only.

questions.q: An exam task says: "Save all lines containing ssh from /etc/services to /root/ssh.txt, in their original order." Which is correct?
questions.explain: Don't sort or change the output unless the task asks. Check with `cat /root/ssh.txt`.

questions.q: Which grep option makes the match case-insensitive?
questions.explain: `grep -i error` matches Error, ERROR and error.

labs.title: Text hunting with grep
labs.scenario: Using /etc/passwd: list users whose shell is /bin/bash, count them, list accounts with UID 0, and save the non-login (nologin) account names to /root/nologin-users.txt.
hints: Use `cut -d: -f1` to keep only the user name field.

labs.title: Regular expressions on a log
labs.scenario: As root, find in /var/log/secure every failed password line, count them, and print only unique source IP addresses. (Create failures first by trying a wrong password with `ssh wronguser@localhost`.)
steps: ssh wronguser@localhost      # type a wrong password a few times

title: Local users and groups
objective: Create, delete and modify local user accounts and groups.

questions.q: How many colon-separated fields does each line in /etc/passwd have?
questions.explain: name:password:UID:GID:comment:home:shell. The password field is `x` because the hash is in /etc/shadow.

questions.q: Where are the password hashes stored?
questions.explain: /etc/shadow is readable only by root. It also stores password-aging fields.

questions.q: On RHEL, which UID does the first regular user account get by default?
questions.explain: UID 0 is root, 1-999 are system accounts. The range comes from /etc/login.defs.

questions.q: Create a user named harry with UID 2000.
questions.explain: Check with `id harry`.

questions.q: Add the existing user natasha to the supplementary group sysmgrs without removing her other groups.
questions.explain: Always use `-a` with `-G`, or the other supplementary groups are removed.

questions.q: What happens if you run `usermod -G sysmgrs natasha` (without -a)?
options: natasha's supplementary groups are replaced by only sysmgrs
sysmgrs is added to her existing groups
questions.explain: `-g` changes the primary group; `-G` sets the full supplementary list.

questions.q: Create the user sarah with a shell that does not allow interactive login.
questions.explain: `/sbin/nologin` and `/usr/sbin/nologin` are the same file on RHEL.

questions.q: Create a group named sysmgrs with GID 3000.
questions.explain: Verify with `getent group sysmgrs`.

questions.q: Which command deletes the user harry together with his home directory and mail spool?
questions.explain: Without `-r`, the home directory stays on disk, owned by a now-unused UID.

questions.q: What does the "user private group" scheme mean on RHEL?
options: Each new user gets a primary group with the same name as the user
Every user joins the users group
Users cannot belong to more than one group
questions.explain: That's why `useradd harry` also creates a group called harry.

labs.title: Exam-style user setup
labs.scenario: Create group sysmgrs. Create users natasha and harry with sysmgrs as a supplementary group. Create user sarah with a non-interactive shell who is not a member of sysmgrs. Set the password of all three to "Rhcsa@2026".
steps: for u in natasha harry sarah; do echo 'Rhcsa@2026' | passwd --stdin $u; done
verify: id natasha; id harry; id sarah

labs.title: Modify accounts
labs.scenario: Change harry's comment to "Harry Potter", move his home to /home/hpotter (moving the files too), lock sarah's account, then unlock it again. Finally rename group sysmgrs to sysadmins and back.
steps: grep sarah /etc/shadow      # a ! appears before the hash

title: Passwords, aging and sudo
objective: Change passwords and adjust password aging; configure privileged access.

questions.q: What does `chage -M 90 harry` set?
options: harry must change his password at most every 90 days
harry must wait 90 days before changing his password
harry gets a warning 90 days before expiry
questions.explain: -M max days, -m min days, -W warning days, -I inactive days, -E account expiry date.

questions.q: Force harry to change his password at his next login.
questions.explain: Setting the last-change date to 0 means the password counts as already expired.

questions.q: Make natasha's account expire on 2026-12-31.
questions.explain: The account (not just the password) stops working after this date.

questions.q: Which file sets the default password-aging values for users created in the future?
questions.explain: Look for PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS and PASS_WARN_AGE.

questions.q: You edit PASS_MAX_DAYS in /etc/login.defs. Which accounts does it affect?
options: Only accounts created after the change
questions.explain: For existing users, run `chage` on each one.

questions.q: Show the password-aging information for harry.
questions.explain: It shows last change, expiry, min, max and warning days in readable form.

questions.q: Set sarah's password to Secret123 without an interactive prompt.
questions.explain: `--stdin` is a RHEL passwd option; it's handy in scripts and exam tasks.

questions.q: What is the safe way to edit sudo rules?
options: Use visudo, or put a file in /etc/sudoers.d/ and check it with visudo -c
questions.explain: visudo checks the syntax before saving. A broken sudoers file can lock everyone out of sudo.

questions.q: Which sudoers line lets members of sysmgrs run any command as root without a password?
questions.explain: `%` marks a group. Without the `%`, sudo treats the name as a user.

questions.q: On RHEL, members of which group get full sudo access by default?
questions.explain: /etc/sudoers contains `%wheel ALL=(ALL) ALL`. Add a user with `usermod -aG wheel user`.

questions.q: What is the difference between `su harry` and `su - harry`?
options: `su -` starts a login shell with harry's full environment and home directory
`su -` does not ask for a password
`su` without the dash only works for root
questions.explain: Prefer `su -` so PATH and variables match the target user.

labs.title: Password policy task
labs.scenario: Make passwords of all NEW users expire after 30 days. For the existing user harry, set maximum password age to 60 days with a 7-day warning, and force him to change his password at next login. Make natasha's account expire on 2026-12-31.
verify: useradd testuser && chage -l testuser | grep Maximum

labs.title: Configure privileged access
labs.scenario: Members of sysmgrs must run all commands as root without a password. User alex may only run `systemctl` as root (with a password). Use files in /etc/sudoers.d and check the syntax.
verify: su - natasha -c 'sudo -n id'      # should print uid=0 with no password prompt

title: Standard permissions
objective: List, set and change ugo/rwx permissions and ownership.

questions.q: What is `rwxr-x---` in octal?
questions.explain: r=4, w=2, x=1 per group of three: 7 (rwx), 5 (r-x), 0 (---).

questions.q: What does the x (execute) permission mean on a directory?
options: You can enter the directory and reach files inside it
You can run every script inside it
questions.explain: r on a directory lets you list names; x lets you enter or traverse; w lets you create and delete entries (it needs x too).

questions.q: What permission do you need to delete a file?
options: Write and execute on the directory that contains it
Read and write on the file
questions.explain: Deleting changes the directory, not the file. The sticky bit changes this rule.

questions.q: Add write permission for the group on report.txt using symbolic mode.
questions.explain: Symbolic mode: who (u g o a), operator (+ - =), permissions (r w x).

questions.q: Set script.sh to rwxr-xr-x using octal mode.
questions.explain: 7 = rwx, 5 = r-x.

questions.q: Make harry the owner and sysmgrs the group of /data in one command.
questions.explain: `chown :group file` changes only the group, same as `chgrp`.

questions.q: Change the group of /shared and everything inside it to sysmgrs.
questions.explain: `-R` applies the change recursively.

questions.q: Who can change which user owns a file?
options: Any member of the file's group
questions.explain: A regular owner can change the group, but only to a group they belong to.

questions.q: In `ls -l` output `-rw-r--r--.`, what does the trailing `.` mean?
options: The file has an SELinux context and no ACL
The file is a hard link
questions.explain: A `+` in that spot means the file has an ACL. Check with `getfacl`.

questions.q: Remove all permissions for "others" on secret.txt without touching owner and group permissions.
questions.explain: `=` with nothing after it sets that class to no permissions.

labs.title: Permissions workout
labs.scenario: Create /srv/project owned by harry and group sysmgrs. Owner: full access. Group: read and enter only. Others: nothing. Inside, create plan.txt readable and writable only by the owner. Test access as natasha and sarah.

labs.title: Fix a script that will not run
labs.scenario: Create /usr/local/bin/hello.sh containing `echo Hello $USER`. Run it and read the error. Fix the permissions so every user can run it but only root can edit it.

title: Special permissions, umask and ACLs
objective: Manage default file permissions and diagnose and correct file permission problems.

questions.q: What does the SGID bit do on a directory?
options: New files created in it get the directory's group
Only the group owner may delete files in it
Files inside it run with group privileges
Group members get write access automatically
questions.explain: This is how you build shared team directories.

questions.q: What does the sticky bit do on a directory such as /tmp?
options: Users can only delete their own files, even with write permission on the directory
Files are never deleted at reboot
New files inherit the directory's owner
questions.explain: /tmp shows `drwxrwxrwt`. In octal the sticky bit is 1, e.g. `chmod 1777`.

questions.q: Set the SGID bit on /home/managers using symbolic mode.
questions.explain: Octal version: `chmod 2770 /home/managers` (2 = SGID, 4 = SUID, 1 = sticky).

questions.q: With umask 027, what permissions does a newly created regular file get?
questions.explain: Files start from 666, directories from 777, then the umask bits are removed: 666-027 = 640, 777-027 = 750.

questions.q: Set the umask of your current shell so new files are 600 and new directories 700.
questions.explain: Run `umask` with no argument to see the current value.

questions.q: How do you make a user's umask survive logout and reboot?
options: Put the umask command in that user's ~/.bashrc or ~/.bash_profile
Set it with chmod on the home directory
questions.explain: For every user, use a script in /etc/profile.d/ instead.

questions.q: Give user natasha read and write access to /var/tmp/fstab using an ACL.
questions.explain: View the result with `getfacl /var/tmp/fstab`.

questions.q: Use an ACL so that user harry has no access at all to /var/tmp/fstab.
questions.explain: A named-user ACL entry takes priority over the "other" permissions.

questions.q: `ls -l /usr/bin/passwd` shows `-rwsr-xr-x`. What does the `s` mean?
options: SUID: the program runs with the privileges of its owner (root)
questions.explain: This is how normal users can update /etc/shadow through passwd. A capital `S` means SUID is set but execute is not.

questions.q: A user cannot open /data/reports/q1.txt even though the file is mode 644. What is the most likely cause?
options: A parent directory is missing the x permission for that user
The user needs to be in the wheel group
The file needs the sticky bit
questions.explain: Check every directory on the path, e.g. `namei -l /data/reports/q1.txt`. Also check ACLs and SELinux.

labs.title: Collaborative directory (exam classic)
labs.scenario: Create /home/managers. Group owner: sysmgrs. Members of sysmgrs get read, write and access; others get no access. Files created inside must automatically belong to sysmgrs.

labs.title: File ACLs (exam classic)
labs.scenario: Copy /etc/fstab to /var/tmp/fstab. Owner root, group root, not executable by anyone. natasha can read and write, harry has no access, everyone else can read.

title: Processes and signals
objective: Identify CPU and memory intensive processes and kill processes; manage jobs.

questions.q: Which signal does `kill PID` send when you give no signal?
questions.explain: SIGTERM asks the program to exit cleanly. Use `kill -9` only when it refuses.

questions.q: Which signal can a process NOT catch or ignore?
questions.explain: SIGKILL and SIGSTOP are handled by the kernel directly.

questions.q: List all processes sorted by CPU usage, highest first.
questions.explain: Use `--sort=-%mem` to sort by memory instead.

questions.q: Kill every process owned by user harry.
questions.explain: `pgrep -u harry` lists the PIDs first so you can see what will be killed.

questions.q: In top, which key sorts processes by memory usage?
questions.explain: P sorts by CPU, M by memory, k kills a PID, r renices, q quits.

questions.q: Start `sleep 1000` as a background job.
questions.explain: The shell prints the job number and PID. `jobs` lists background jobs.

questions.q: What does Ctrl+Z do to the program running in the foreground?
options: Stops (suspends) it; `bg` resumes it in the background
Moves it to the background while it keeps running
questions.explain: Ctrl+C sends SIGINT to end it. Ctrl+Z sends SIGTSTP to pause it.

questions.q: Bring job number 1 back to the foreground.
questions.explain: `bg %1` resumes it in the background instead. `kill %1` sends it SIGTERM.

questions.q: A process shows state `D` in ps. What does that mean?
options: Uninterruptible sleep, usually waiting for disk or network I/O
It is running on a CPU
questions.explain: R running, S sleeping, T stopped, Z zombie, D uninterruptible sleep.

labs.title: Find and stop CPU hogs
labs.scenario: Start three CPU-heavy processes with `sha1sum /dev/zero &`. Find them with ps sorted by CPU and with top. Kill one by PID with SIGTERM, and kill the other two by name.
steps: for i in 1 2 3; do sha1sum /dev/zero & done
top          # press P, note a PID, press q

labs.title: Find the biggest memory users
labs.scenario: Save the 5 processes using the most memory (with PID, user, %MEM and command) to /root/topmem.txt.

labs.title: Job control drill
labs.scenario: Start `sleep 500` and `sleep 600` in the background and `sleep 700` in the foreground. Suspend the foreground job, resume it in the background, bring job 2 to the foreground and end it with Ctrl+C, then kill the rest by job number.

labs.title: Pause and resume a process with signals
labs.scenario: As harry, start `sleep 900`. As root, stop it with SIGSTOP, confirm the state is T, resume it with SIGCONT, then kill it with SIGKILL.

title: Controlling services with systemd
objective: Start, stop and check services; configure automatic startup.

questions.q: Start httpd now and also enable it at boot, in one command.
questions.explain: `enable` alone only affects the next boot. `--now` also starts it.

questions.q: What does `systemctl mask atd` do?
options: Links the unit to /dev/null so it cannot be started at all, even manually
Disables it at boot but still allows manual start
Stops it and deletes its unit file
questions.explain: Undo with `systemctl unmask atd`.

questions.q: Check whether sshd is enabled to start at boot.
questions.explain: `systemctl is-active sshd` tells you whether it's running now.

questions.q: List all units that are in a failed state.
questions.explain: Then run `systemctl status <unit>` and `journalctl -u <unit>` for details.

questions.q: What is the difference between `systemctl reload` and `systemctl restart`?
options: reload tells the service to re-read its config without stopping; restart stops and starts it
reload also enables the service at boot
restart only works if reload fails
questions.explain: Not every service supports reload; `systemctl reload-or-restart` covers both cases.

questions.q: You create or edit a unit file under /etc/systemd/system. What must you run next?
questions.explain: systemd caches unit files. daemon-reload makes it read them again.

questions.q: Where should administrators put their own unit files and overrides?
questions.explain: Package units live in /usr/lib/systemd/system. Files in /etc take priority. `systemctl edit unit` creates a drop-in override for you.

questions.q: Stop the atd service and stop it starting at boot, in one command.
questions.explain: Confirm with `systemctl status atd`.

questions.q: `systemctl status sshd` shows "Loaded: ... enabled; preset: enabled" and "Active: active (running)". What does that mean?
options: sshd is running now and will start at boot
sshd is running but will not start at boot
sshd starts at boot but is not running now
questions.explain: "enabled" is the boot setting, "active" is the current state. They are separate.

labs.title: Install and run a web server
labs.scenario: Install httpd, start it and enable it at boot, allow HTTP through the firewall, put "Hello RHCSA" in /var/www/html/index.html and fetch it with curl.
verify: systemctl is-enabled httpd; systemctl is-active httpd

labs.title: Mask and unmask a service
labs.scenario: Mask atd, try to start it and read the error, then unmask it and make sure it is running and enabled.
steps: systemctl start atd       # Unit atd.service is masked.

labs.title: Explore units
labs.scenario: List all installed service unit files and their boot state, show what multi-user.target pulls in, and print the unit file of sshd.

labs.title: Write your own service
labs.scenario: Create /usr/local/bin/heartbeat.sh that writes "alive" to the journal every 30 seconds in a loop. Create heartbeat.service to run it, enable it at boot, and read its messages in the journal.
steps: printf '#!/bin/bash\nwhile true; do echo alive; sleep 30; done\n' > /usr/local/bin/heartbeat.sh

title: Configure and secure SSH
objective: Access remote systems using SSH and configure key-based authentication.

questions.q: Generate a new SSH key pair with the default settings.
questions.explain: Keys are saved in ~/.ssh/. The .pub file is the public key you share.

questions.q: Copy your public key to the account harry on host servera.
questions.explain: It appends your key to ~harry/.ssh/authorized_keys and sets safe permissions.

questions.q: On the server, which file lists the public keys allowed to log in to an account?
questions.explain: known_hosts on the client stores the server fingerprints you have accepted.

questions.q: Which permissions does sshd expect on ~/.ssh and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys?
options: 700 on the directory and 600 on the file
questions.explain: If they are too open, sshd ignores the key (StrictModes) and falls back to a password.

questions.q: How do you stop root from logging in over SSH?
options: Set `PermitRootLogin no` in the sshd config, then reload sshd
Set root's shell to nologin in /etc/ssh/ssh_config
questions.explain: On RHEL 9 and 10 you can put the setting in a file under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/. /etc/ssh/ssh_config is the client config, not the server.

questions.q: Check the sshd configuration for syntax errors before reloading.
questions.explain: No output means the syntax is valid. Then run `systemctl reload sshd`.

questions.q: Run `hostname` on servera as student without opening an interactive shell.
questions.explain: The command runs remotely and the output comes back to your terminal.

questions.q: What is OpenSSH's built-in default for PermitRootLogin, which RHEL 9 and 10 use?
options: prohibit-password: root can log in with a key but not with a password
questions.explain: Exam tasks often need root password login between exam nodes, or a key. Read the task carefully.

questions.q: Where are the SSH server's own host keys stored?
questions.explain: If a host is reinstalled, its host key changes and clients warn you. Remove the old line with `ssh-keygen -R host`.

labs.title: Key-based login between two machines
labs.scenario: On node1 as student, generate a key pair and set up key-based login to student@node2. Confirm you can run a command on node2 with no password prompt.
verify: ssh -o PasswordAuthentication=no student@node2 true && echo KEY-OK

labs.title: Harden the SSH server
labs.scenario: On node2: stop root logging in over SSH and stop password logins for everyone. Make sure your key login works BEFORE you reload sshd, then test both.
hints: Settings in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf are read first, so the first value set wins.

labs.title: Remote commands and quick copies
labs.scenario: From node1, save the output of `df -h` on node2 to /root/node2-disk.txt on node1, and copy node2's /etc/os-release into /tmp on node1 in one command each.

labs.title: Use ssh-agent with a passphrase
labs.scenario: Create a second key ~/.ssh/lab_key with a passphrase, install it on node2, and load it into ssh-agent so you type the passphrase only once.

title: System logs and the journal
objective: Locate and interpret system log files and journals; preserve system journals.

questions.q: Show journal entries for the sshd service only.
questions.explain: Add `-f` to follow, `-n 20` for the last 20 lines, `--since today` to limit time.

questions.q: Show only messages of priority err or worse from the current boot.
questions.explain: `-p` includes that level and everything more severe.

questions.q: Show journal messages from the last hour.
questions.explain: You can also give dates: `--since "2026-10-01 09:00" --until "2026-10-01 10:00"`.

questions.q: Which journald setting keeps the journal across reboots?
questions.explain: With the default Storage=auto, the journal is only kept if /var/log/journal exists. Otherwise it stays in /run/log/journal and is lost at reboot.

questions.q: Which file holds authentication and security messages on RHEL?
questions.explain: /var/log/auth.log is the Debian and Ubuntu name. SELinux denials go to /var/log/audit/audit.log.

questions.q: Send the test message "hello from logger" to syslog with priority user.notice.
questions.explain: Check it with `tail /var/log/messages` or `journalctl -n 5`.

questions.q: What does the rsyslog rule `authpriv.*  /var/log/secure` mean?
options: Messages of every priority from the authpriv facility go to /var/log/secure
questions.explain: Rule format: facility.priority followed by the target. Drop-in rules go in /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf.

questions.q: Which list orders syslog priorities from most to least severe?
options: emerg, alert, crit, err, warning, notice, info, debug
debug, info, notice, warning, err, crit, alert, emerg
crit, emerg, alert, err, warning, info, notice, debug
err, warning, info, debug, notice, crit, alert, emerg
questions.explain: Numbers 0 to 7 in that same order.

questions.q: List every boot the journal has records for.
questions.explain: Only the current boot is listed unless the journal is persistent. `journalctl -b -1` shows the previous boot.

labs.title: Preserve the journal (exam objective)
labs.scenario: Configure the journal so it survives reboots. Reboot, then prove that the previous boot's messages are still there.
verify: journalctl --list-boots      # two or more boots listed

labs.title: Custom rsyslog rule
labs.scenario: Send messages of every facility at priority debug and above to a new file /var/log/messages-debug. Test it with logger.
steps: logger -p user.debug "Debug test from RHCSA practice"

labs.title: Investigate failed logins
labs.scenario: Make a few failed SSH logins to localhost, then use journalctl to show today's failed sshd attempts and count them.

labs.title: Filter the journal by fields
labs.scenario: Show journal entries for UID 1000 only, then only entries from the sshd command, then one entry in full verbose form.

title: Time synchronization
objective: Configure time service clients and time zones.

questions.q: Show the current time, time zone and whether NTP sync is active.
questions.explain: Look for "System clock synchronized: yes" and "NTP service: active".

questions.q: Set the system time zone to Asia/Kolkata.
questions.explain: This updates the /etc/localtime symlink.

questions.q: List the available time zones that contain "Asia".
questions.explain: `tzselect` asks you questions and suggests a zone name.

questions.q: Which file configures the chrony NTP client on RHEL?
questions.explain: RHEL uses chronyd. ntpd and timesyncd are not the RHEL defaults.

questions.q: Which chrony.conf line syncs from classroom.example.com and speeds up the first sync?
questions.explain: Use `server` for one host and `pool` for a pool name that resolves to many hosts.

questions.q: Apply your chrony.conf changes.
questions.explain: Also make sure it starts at boot: `systemctl enable chronyd`.

questions.q: Show the time sources chrony is using.
questions.explain: `-v` adds a legend that explains each column.

questions.q: In `chronyc sources` output, what does `^*` before a server mean?
options: It is the source chrony is currently synchronized to
The server is too far off and was rejected
The server is a local reference clock
questions.explain: `^?` means not reachable yet. Wait a minute after a restart.

questions.q: What does `timedatectl set-ntp true` do on RHEL?
options: Enables and starts chronyd so the clock is synced over the network
Syncs the time once and exits
Switches the time zone to UTC
questions.explain: `set-ntp false` stops and disables chronyd.

labs.title: Configure an NTP client (exam classic)
labs.scenario: Make node1 an NTP client of node2 (or of classroom.example.com in class). Remove the default pool line and confirm node1 syncs to it.

labs.title: Turn node2 into an NTP server
labs.scenario: Let node2 answer NTP requests from your lab subnet and open the firewall for it, so node1's client task has a server.
steps: # add: local stratum 10  (serve time even without internet)
verify: chronyc clients      # run after node1 has synced

labs.title: Time zones and manual time
labs.scenario: Set the time zone to America/New_York, turn off NTP, set the clock to 2026-12-25 10:00:00, look at the result, then set the zone back to Asia/Kolkata and turn NTP on again.

title: Networking: IPv4 and hostname
objective: Configure IPv4 addresses, hostname and hostname resolution with NetworkManager.

questions.q: Show all connection profiles that NetworkManager knows about.
questions.explain: `nmcli dev status` shows the devices and which profile each one uses.

questions.q: Show the IP addresses on all interfaces.
questions.explain: `ip -br a` gives one short line per interface.

questions.q: Where does NetworkManager on RHEL 9 and 10 store connection profiles?
questions.explain: ifcfg files are the old RHEL 8 format. After editing a keyfile by hand, run `nmcli con reload`.

questions.q: On connection "eth0", set the static address 192.168.100.10/24 with gateway 192.168.100.1 and manual method.
accept: nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.addresses 192.168.100.10/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.100.1 ipv4.method manual
nmcli connection modify eth0 ipv4.addresses 192.168.100.10/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.100.1 ipv4.method manual
nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.100.10/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.100.1
questions.explain: Without `ipv4.method manual`, the profile may keep using DHCP.

questions.q: When do settings changed with `nmcli con mod` take effect?
options: When the connection is activated again, e.g. `nmcli con up eth0`
questions.explain: If you work over SSH and change the IP, your session drops. Use the console.

questions.q: Set the hostname permanently to node1.lab.example.com.
questions.explain: This writes /etc/hostname. Check it with `hostnamectl` or `hostname`.

questions.q: Which file maps host names to IP addresses locally, before DNS is asked?
questions.explain: The lookup order is set by the `hosts:` line in /etc/nsswitch.conf.

questions.q: Set DNS server 192.168.100.1 on connection eth0.
questions.explain: NetworkManager then writes it to /etc/resolv.conf. Don't edit resolv.conf by hand.

questions.q: Which command lists listening TCP and UDP ports with the process using each one?
questions.explain: t = TCP, u = UDP, l = listening, p = process, n = numeric ports.

labs.title: Static IPv4 network (exam classic)
labs.scenario: On node1, configure the existing connection with IP 192.168.122.11/24, gateway 192.168.122.1 and DNS 192.168.122.1 (adjust to your lab subnet). Set the hostname to node1.lab.example.com. It must all survive a reboot.
steps: nmcli con mod "<profile>" ipv4.addresses 192.168.122.11/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.122.1 ipv4.dns 192.168.122.1 ipv4.method manual connection.autoconnect yes

labs.title: Create a new connection profile
labs.scenario: Create a profile "static-lab" for your interface with a static address, and keep the DHCP profile too. Switch between them and check the address each time.
steps: nmcli con add con-name static-lab type ethernet ifname <dev> ipv4.addresses 192.168.122.50/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.122.1 ipv4.dns 192.168.122.1 ipv4.method manual

labs.title: Add a second IP address
labs.scenario: Add 10.0.0.11/24 as an extra address to your main profile without removing the first one.

labs.title: Local name resolution
labs.scenario: Add node1 and node2 (short and full names) to /etc/hosts on both machines. Resolve and ping by name.

title: Networking: IPv6, DNS and troubleshooting
objective: Configure IPv6 addresses, name resolution and network services at boot.

questions.q: Give connection eth0 the static IPv6 address fd00:10::10/64 with the manual method.
accept: nmcli con mod eth0 ipv6.addresses fd00:10::10/64 ipv6.method manual
nmcli connection modify eth0 ipv6.addresses fd00:10::10/64 ipv6.method manual
nmcli con mod eth0 ipv6.method manual ipv6.addresses fd00:10::10/64
questions.explain: Add `ipv6.gateway fd00:10::1` if the task gives a gateway, then `nmcli con up eth0`.

questions.q: What is the IPv6 loopback address?
questions.explain: `::` on its own means the all-zero (unspecified) address.

questions.q: Addresses beginning with fe80:: are what kind of IPv6 address?
options: Link-local, created automatically on every IPv6 interface
Global addresses routed on the internet
questions.explain: Your static address shows as "scope global" in `ip a` next to the fe80:: link-local one.

title: RPM and DNF packages
objective: Install and remove RPM software packages; query the RPM database.

questions.q: Find which installed package owns the file /etc/ssh/sshd_config.
questions.explain: `rpm -qf` only looks at installed packages; `dnf provides` also searches repositories.

questions.q: List the configuration files that belong to the chrony package.
questions.explain: -qc lists config files, -qd docs, -ql all files, -qi package info.

questions.q: Find which package provides the semanage command, even if it is not installed yet.
questions.explain: The answer is policycoreutils-python-utils. You will need it for SELinux tasks.

questions.q: What is the advantage of `dnf install ./pkg.rpm` over `rpm -ivh pkg.rpm`?
options: dnf also installs the dependencies from the enabled repositories
questions.explain: rpm only reports missing dependencies and stops.

questions.q: List every installed package with "http" in its name.
questions.explain: rpm -qa prints every installed package.

questions.q: What does `dnf history undo 12` do?
options: Reverses the changes made by transaction 12
questions.explain: `dnf history` lists transactions and `dnf history info 12` shows one.

questions.q: Install the package group "Development Tools".
questions.explain: `dnf group list` shows the available groups.

questions.q: What happens to the running kernel when `dnf update` installs a newer kernel?
options: The new kernel is added next to the old ones and used after a reboot
The old kernel is removed immediately
Kernels are never updated by dnf
questions.explain: Kernels are "install-only" packages, so you can boot an older one from GRUB if the new one fails.

questions.q: Remove the httpd package.
questions.explain: dnf also removes packages that depend on httpd. Read the list before confirming.

labs.title: Query the RPM database
labs.scenario: Answer with rpm commands only: which package owns /usr/bin/ls, which files does openssh-server install, where are its config files, and when was it installed?

labs.title: Install from a local RPM file
labs.scenario: Download the tree package as an .rpm file into /root/rpms without installing it. Inspect the file, then install it from the local file.

labs.title: Use dnf history
labs.scenario: Install the packages zsh and tmux in one transaction, find that transaction in the history, then undo it.

labs.title: Work with package groups
labs.scenario: List the available groups, show what "Development Tools" contains, and install it.

title: Repositories and Flatpak
objective: Configure access to RPM repositories and Flatpak repositories; install and remove Flatpak packages.

questions.q: Where do DNF repository definitions go?
questions.explain: Every file in /etc/yum.repos.d/ ending in `.repo` is read. The file name does not matter.

questions.q: Which set of lines is enough for a working repository section?
options: [id], name, baseurl, enabled=1 and gpgcheck (0 or 1 with a gpgkey)
questions.explain: A typo in baseurl is the most common exam mistake. Test with `dnf repolist` and install a package.

questions.q: Add a repository for http://repo.lab.example.com/BaseOS with dnf config-manager.
questions.explain: It writes a new .repo file. If the task asks for gpgcheck=0, edit the file afterwards.

questions.q: List the enabled repositories.
questions.explain: `dnf repolist all` includes the disabled ones.

questions.q: What is the baseurl for a BaseOS repository on a DVD mounted at /mnt/iso?
questions.explain: `file://` plus the absolute path `/mnt/iso/...` gives three slashes.

questions.q: Add the Flathub remote only if it is not already configured.
questions.explain: In the exam, use the remote name and URL the task gives you.

questions.q: List the configured Flatpak remotes.
questions.explain: `flatpak remote-ls <remote>` lists the apps a remote offers.

questions.q: Install the app org.gnome.Calculator from the flathub remote.
questions.explain: `flatpak list` shows installed apps; `flatpak run <app-id>` starts one.

questions.q: Where does `flatpak install` put apps if you do not pass --user?
options: System-wide, for all users (needs admin rights)
questions.explain: `--user` installs just for you, under ~/.local/share/flatpak.

questions.q: Uninstall the org.gnome.Calculator Flatpak app.
questions.explain: `flatpak uninstall --unused` removes runtimes that no app needs any more.

labs.title: Local repository from the RHEL ISO
labs.scenario: Attach the RHEL 10 ISO to your VM. Mount it permanently at /mnt/iso and create /etc/yum.repos.d/local.repo with BaseOS and AppStream repositories from it. Install httpd from it to prove it works.

labs.title: Network repositories (exam style)
labs.scenario: On node2, publish the ISO over HTTP by linking /mnt/iso into /var/www/html/rhel10. Then on node1, configure repos BaseOS and AppStream pointing to http://node2/rhel10/BaseOS and http://node2/rhel10/AppStream.
steps: dnf install -y httpd && systemctl enable --now httpd

labs.title: Flatpak end to end
labs.scenario: Install the flatpak package, add the Flathub remote, search for a calculator app, install it system-wide, list installed apps, and uninstall it. (Needs internet on the VM.)

labs.title: Enable and disable repositories
labs.scenario: Disable the AppStream repo, see that httpd can no longer be found, then enable it again. Also try a single command that ignores it only once.

title: Archives and secure file transfer
objective: Archive, compress, unpack and uncompress files with tar, gzip and bzip2; securely transfer files between systems.

questions.q: Create the gzip-compressed archive /root/etc.tar.gz of /etc.
questions.explain: c = create, z = gzip, f = file name, v = list files as they are added.

questions.q: Create the bzip2-compressed archive /root/local.tar.bz2 of /usr/local.
questions.explain: j = bzip2. The bzip2 package must be installed.

questions.q: Which tar option compresses with xz?
questions.explain: Summary: -z gzip (.gz), -j bzip2 (.bz2), -J xz (.xz).

questions.q: List the contents of /root/etc.tar.gz without extracting it.
questions.explain: Modern tar detects the compression when reading, so -z is optional here.

questions.q: Extract /root/etc.tar.gz into the existing directory /tmp/restore.
questions.explain: `-C` changes to that directory before extracting.

questions.q: tar prints "Removing leading '/' from member names". What does that mean?
options: Paths are stored relative, so extracting never overwrites the original location by accident
You must run tar as root
questions.explain: When you extract, the files go under your current directory (or the -C directory).

questions.q: Copy /etc/hosts into /tmp on serverb, logging in as root over SSH.
questions.explain: Reverse the arguments to copy from the remote host. Add `-r` for directories.

questions.q: What does a trailing slash on the source mean in `rsync -av /var/www/ serverb:/backup/www`?
options: The contents of /var/www are copied into /backup/www, not the www directory itself
rsync deletes files on the target
questions.explain: Without the slash you get /backup/www/www.

questions.q: What does `gzip notes.txt` do?
options: Replaces notes.txt with the compressed notes.txt.gz
questions.explain: Use `gunzip notes.txt.gz` to reverse it, or `gzip -k` to keep the original.

labs.title: Compare compression types
labs.scenario: Archive /etc three times, with gzip, bzip2 and xz, into /root/backups. Compare the sizes and check each file's type.

labs.title: Backup archive (exam classic)
labs.scenario: Create /root/backup.tar.bz2 containing /usr/local, compressed with bzip2. Confirm it is valid and lists the expected files.

labs.title: Restore a single file
labs.scenario: From /root/backups/etc.tar.gz, restore only etc/hosts into /tmp/restore, and compare it with the live file.

labs.title: Move files between nodes
labs.scenario: Copy /root/backup.tar.bz2 from node1 to /tmp on node2 with scp. Sync /etc/yum.repos.d/ from node1 into /root/repos-copy on node2 with rsync. Use sftp to download /etc/hostname from node2.
steps: sftp root@node2      # then: get /etc/hostname   and   bye

title: Accessing file systems and users on consoles
objective: Mount and inspect file systems; log in and switch users in multi-user targets.

questions.q: List all block devices with their filesystem types and UUIDs.
questions.explain: `lsblk` alone shows sizes and mount points.

questions.q: Show free space on mounted filesystems in human-readable units, including the filesystem type.
questions.explain: `df` reports filesystems; `du` reports what files use.

questions.q: Show the total disk space used by /var/log.
questions.explain: -s summary, -h human-readable. `du -h --max-depth=1 /var` lists subdirectories.

questions.q: Mount /dev/vdb1 on /mnt/data for now (not permanently).
questions.explain: For a permanent mount, add a line to /etc/fstab.

questions.q: `umount /mnt/data` says "target is busy". What is the usual cause?
options: A process, maybe your own shell, is using files or has its working directory there
questions.explain: `cd` out of it, then find other users with `lsof /mnt/data` or `fuser -vm /mnt/data`.

questions.q: Show the UUID of /dev/vdb1.
questions.explain: Use the UUID in /etc/fstab. It does not change if disks are renamed.

questions.q: On a text-only system in multi-user.target, how do you reach a second login console?
options: Press Ctrl+Alt+F2 (F2 to F6 give more consoles)
questions.explain: In a VM, send the key combination from the VM window's menu.

questions.q: Which command shows who is logged in and what each person is running?
questions.explain: `who` is shorter, `last` shows past logins.

questions.q: What is the difference between `sudo -i` and `su -`?
options: sudo -i asks for your own password and needs sudo rights; su - asks for root's password
su - only works for regular users

title: Shell scripts: basics
objective: Process script inputs ($1, $2, etc.) and process the output of shell commands within scripts.

questions.q: What should the first line of a bash script be?
questions.explain: This "shebang" line tells the kernel which interpreter runs the file.

questions.q: Make script.sh executable for everyone.
questions.explain: Run it as `./script.sh`, or put it in /usr/local/bin so it's on the PATH.

questions.q: Inside a script, what are $1, $# and $@?
options: The first argument, the number of arguments, and all arguments
The script name, the PID, and the exit code
The first line, the line count, and all lines
The user, the group, and the home directory
questions.explain: $0 is the script's own name. Quote "$@" so arguments with spaces stay intact.

questions.q: What does $? contain?
options: The exit status of the last command (0 means success)
The PID of the last background job
questions.explain: Check it right after the command, because every command overwrites it.

questions.q: Store the output of the `hostname` command in a variable named host.
questions.explain: Prefer $( ); it nests cleanly and is easier to read.

questions.q: What happens with `count = 5` in bash?
options: An error: bash tries to run a command named count
questions.explain: Assignments must have no spaces around the =.

questions.q: What is the difference between "$HOME" and '$HOME'?
options: Double quotes expand the variable; single quotes keep the text literally
Single quotes expand it; double quotes do not
questions.explain: Use double quotes around variables to keep spaces intact and still expand them.

questions.q: Print the number of arguments that were passed to the script.
questions.explain: Useful for checking that the user passed what the script needs.

questions.q: What does `exit 1` do in a script?
options: Ends the script immediately with exit status 1 (failure)
questions.explain: By convention, 0 means success and anything else means an error.

objective: Conditionally execute code and use looping constructs to process files and command-line input.

questions.q: Which test is true when `file` exists and is a regular file?
questions.explain: -e exists (any type), -f regular file, -d directory, -r readable, -x executable, -s not empty.

questions.q: Which is the correct numeric comparison "a is greater than 5"?
questions.explain: Numbers: -eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge. Strings: = and !=. Inside [ ], `>` means redirection.

questions.q: Write a one-line for loop that prints the numbers 1 to 5.
accept: for i in {1..5}; do echo $i; done
for i in $(seq 1 5); do echo $i; done
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do echo $i; done
for i in {1..5}; do echo "$i"; done
questions.explain: Loops can also go over files (`for f in /etc/*.conf`) or command output.

questions.q: What does `while read line; do echo "$line"; done < users.txt` do?
options: Reads users.txt one line at a time into $line
Reads the whole file into one variable
Waits for the user to type a line
questions.explain: This is the safe way to process a list of names from a file.

questions.q: When is `[ -z "$1" ]` true?
options: When $1 is empty or not given
When $1 is a file with size zero
questions.explain: `-n` is the opposite: true when the string is not empty.

questions.q: In `cmd1 && cmd2 || cmd3`, when does cmd3 run?
options: When cmd1 fails, or when cmd1 succeeds and cmd2 fails
questions.explain: && runs the next command on success, || on failure. For clear logic, use if/then/else.

questions.q: Using the test brackets, print "yes" only if /etc/hosts is readable.
questions.explain: `test` and `[ ]` are the same builtin.

questions.q: Which if statement has correct syntax?
options: if [$x = yes] then echo ok fi
questions.explain: Spaces inside the brackets are required. Close with `fi`.

questions.q: Which word ends a case block?
questions.explain: case is spelled backwards; each branch ends with `;;`.

questions.q: Delete at job number 3.

questions.q: What is the order of the five time fields in a crontab line?
options: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week
hour, minute, day of month, month, day of week
minute, hour, month, day of month, day of week

questions.q: What does `*/10 * * * *` mean?

questions.q: What does `30 14 * * 1-5` mean?
options: At 14:30 on days 1 to 5 of the month
At 30 minutes past 2 AM, Monday to Friday
questions.explain: Day of week: 0 or 7 = Sunday, 1 = Monday ... 6 = Saturday.

questions.q: How are lines in /etc/crontab and /etc/cron.d/* different from a user crontab?
options: They have an extra field, the user name, before the command
They use seconds instead of minutes

objective: Schedule tasks using systemd timer units; manage temporary files.

questions.q: Which unit files do you need for a systemd timer job?
options: A .timer unit and a .service unit with the same name
A .service unit with a Schedule= line
questions.explain: The timer starts the matching service. You can point it elsewhere with Unit=.

questions.q: What does `OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:00:00` mean?
questions.explain: Format: DayOfWeek Year-Month-Day Hour:Minute:Second. `daily` means `*-*-* 00:00:00`.

questions.q: List all timers with their next and last run times.
questions.explain: `--all` also shows inactive timers.

questions.q: Check which times the calendar expression "Mon..Fri *-*-* 09:00" matches.

questions.q: What does `Persistent=true` do in a timer?
options: If the system was off at the scheduled time, the job runs soon after the next boot
The timer can never be disabled
questions.explain: This is similar to what anacron does for cron.

questions.q: Which target should a timer's [Install] section name?
questions.explain: Then `systemctl enable --now name.timer`. Enable the timer, not the service.

questions.q: Enable and start backup.timer now.

questions.q: What does `OnBootSec=15min` mean in a timer?
options: Run the service 15 minutes after the system boots
Wait 15 minutes before the service stops

questions.q: What does the tmpfiles.d line `d /run/myapp 0755 root root 1d` do?

questions.q: Can `setenforce` turn SELinux off completely?
options: No, it only switches between enforcing and permissive
Only as root in rescue mode

questions.q: What happens to an action the policy would deny, in permissive mode?
options: It is allowed, but the denial is still logged

questions.q: Where are SELinux AVC denials logged?

options: It keeps partitions aligned and leaves room for the GPT header
It makes the partition faster to format

questions.q: Show the partition table of /dev/vdb.

mount point, device, type, options, fsck order, dump
device, type, mount point, options, dump, fsck order
UUID, label, mount point, type, options, dump

/dev names are not allowed in fstab

options: Use `set -o noclobber`, then `>` refuses to overwrite existing files
questions.explain: Most exam tasks just want `>`. Know the options anyway.

labs.title: Links and copies
labs.scenario: Create a hard link /root/fstab.hard and a symbolic link /root/fstab.soft, both to /etc/fstab. Copy /etc/hosts to /root/hosts.bak keeping all attributes. Show the inode numbers.

labs.title: Extract lines to a file
labs.scenario: Put every line of /etc/services that contains the word "ftp" into /root/ftp-lines, in the original order. Then put only the service names (first column) of those lines, without duplicates, into /root/ftp-names.

labs.title: Find and copy by owner
labs.scenario: Create user jacques and give him files in /tmp and /var/tmp. Find all files owned by jacques and copy them into /root/found (create it).
