labs.scenario: Archive /etc/ssh into /root/ssh.tar.gz, /root/ssh.tar.bz2 and /root/ssh.tar.xz. Extract the bzip2 one into /tmp/sshcheck and compare it with the original.

labs.title: Documentation hunt against the clock
labs.scenario: In under 5 minutes, using only local docs, find: the fstab option that lets a mount fail without stopping the boot, the nmcli example for a static IP, and the rich-rule syntax to reject a source address.
verify: you found all three from local documentation

title: Review: users, groups and permissions
objective: Mixed exam-style practice on accounts, aging, sudo, special permissions and ACLs.

questions.q: A task says user "manalo" must have UID 3533 and password "flectrag". Which pair of commands does it?
options: useradd -u 3533 manalo; echo flectrag | passwd --stdin manalo
questions.explain: `useradd -p` expects an already hashed password, so don't use it with plain text.

questions.q: New users must get passwords that expire after 20 days. What do you change?
questions.explain: Only future accounts are affected. Existing accounts keep their settings.

questions.q: A shared directory must let group members delete only their own files. Which mode fits?
options: 3770 (SGID and sticky bit, rwx for owner and group)
questions.explain: 2 = SGID for group inheritance, 1 = sticky for "delete only your own".

questions.q: Allow members of the group admins to run any command as any user via sudo, with a password.
questions.explain: Then `visudo -c` to check the syntax.

questions.q: A user's umask must give new files 640 and directories 750. Which umask?
Remove all ACL entries from /var/tmp/fstab.
questions.explain: `setfacl -x u:natasha /var/tmp/fstab` removes just one entry.

questions.q: Where do you put a umask for every user on the system?
questions.explain: UMASK in /etc/login.defs affects home directories created by useradd and some login paths. A profile.d script covers shells.

questions.q: Give new files created in /srv/team a default ACL granting user harry rwx.
questions.explain: Default ACLs only work on directories and apply to files created later.

labs.title: Account setup from a spec
labs.scenario: Create group "developers" with GID 5000. Create users dev1 and dev2 (secondary group developers), and user auditor with UID 4000 and no interactive shell. Set all passwords to "Rhcsa@2026". dev1 must change the password at first login.
steps: useradd -G developers dev1; useradd -G developers dev2
for u in dev1 dev2 auditor; do echo 'Rhcsa@2026' | passwd --stdin $u; done
verify: id dev1; id dev2; id auditor; chage -l dev1 | head -1

labs.title: Team directory with SGID and sticky bit
labs.scenario: Create /srv/devshare owned by root:developers. Members can read, write and enter; others get nothing. New files belong to developers, and members can delete only their own files.
verify: su - dev1 -c 'touch /srv/devshare/f1'; su - dev2 -c 'rm /srv/devshare/f1'   # not permitted

labs.title: Password aging for existing and new users
labs.scenario: New users' passwords expire after 45 days with a 5-day warning. dev2's password expires after 30 days, and auditor's account expires on 2027-03-31.

labs.title: Umask for one user
labs.scenario: New files created by dev1 must have mode 600 and new directories 700. It must survive logout.
verify: su - dev1 -c 'touch f; mkdir d; ls -ld f d'

labs.title: Fix a permission problem
labs.scenario: Run this setup: `mkdir -p /data/reports && echo q1 > /data/reports/q1.txt && chmod 700 /data && chmod 644 /data/reports/q1.txt`. dev1 must be able to read q1.txt but not list or change anything else in /data. Find and fix the problem with the smallest change.
steps: chmod o+x /data      # traverse only, no listing
verify: su - dev1 -c 'cat /data/reports/q1.txt'; su - dev1 -c 'ls /data'   # read works, ls denied

title: Review: storage I
objective: Mixed exam-style practice on partitions, swap and creating LVM storage.

questions.q: An exam disk already has partitions and a mounted filesystem. A task says to add a partition. What must you avoid?
options: Creating a new partition table (mklabel) on that disk
Starting the partition after the last one
questions.explain: mklabel erases every existing partition on the disk.

questions.q: Which command shows free space left on /dev/vdb in parted?
questions.explain: Start your new partition where the free space begins.

questions.q: The task wants a 1 GiB LV "exam" and the VG uses 32 MiB extents. How many extents is that?
questions.explain: 1024 MiB / 32 MiB = 32 extents. Using -L 1G gives the same result.

questions.q: Create the volume group datavg from /dev/vdb3 and /dev/vdc1 with 8 MiB extents.
questions.explain: Both devices must be PVs, or vgcreate initializes them for you.

questions.q: After adding a swap line to /etc/fstab, how do you test it without rebooting?
questions.explain: `mount -a` ignores swap entries.

questions.q: Show the UUID of every block device in one command.
questions.explain: Copy UUIDs carefully. A single wrong character stops the boot.

questions.q: Which fstab line mounts an XFS logical volume by its device mapper path?
questions.explain: /dev/datavg/exam works too.

questions.q: What should you always do after editing /etc/fstab, before rebooting?
options: Run systemctl daemon-reload and mount -a (and swapon -a for swap) to test it
questions.explain: A broken fstab found at boot means emergency mode.

labs.title: Add storage without touching existing data
labs.scenario: On a disk that already holds partitions, add a 400 MiB XFS partition mounted at /mnt/extra by UUID, and a 300 MiB swap partition active at boot. Existing partitions and swap must stay untouched.

labs.title: LVM from scratch with extents
labs.scenario: Create VG examvg with 32 MiB extents on a new partition. Create LV exam of 20 extents, format it XFS, and mount it at /exam at boot.

labs.title: LVM swap
labs.scenario: Add a 512 MiB swap LV in examvg that is active at boot.

labs.title: Reboot test
labs.scenario: Reboot and confirm every mount and swap area from today came back. If the boot fails, fix it from emergency mode.

title: Review: storage II
objective: Mixed exam-style practice on extending storage, VFAT, NFS and autofs.

questions.q: The task says "extend the /exam filesystem to 900 MiB". The VG has only 200 MiB free. What do you do first?
options: Add a new PV to the VG with vgextend
Extend it by 200 MiB and stop
questions.explain: Read the whole task: it may also tell you which disk to use.

questions.q: Why is `lvextend -r` safer in an exam than lvextend followed by a separate grow command?
options: You cannot forget to grow the filesystem
It works on unmounted XFS only
questions.explain: Always confirm with `df -h` afterwards.

questions.q: Mount node2:/shares/docs at /mnt/docs at boot. Write the fstab line.
questions.explain: Test with `mount -a` and `findmnt /mnt/docs`.

questions.q: For an autofs indirect map at /rhome, which directory must NOT contain pre-made subdirectories?
questions.explain: autofs manages /rhome. Any leftovers there confuse the mounts.

questions.q: autofs is configured but `cd /rhome/remoteuser1` fails. What do you check?
options: That autofs is running, the map spelling, the export on the server, and the journal for autofs
questions.explain: `showmount -e node2` confirms the export exists.

questions.q: Format /dev/vdb6 as VFAT with the label USBDATA in one command.
questions.explain: For VFAT the label option is -n; for XFS and ext4 it is -L.

questions.q: What does "configure systems to mount file systems at boot by UUID or label" mean for your fstab lines?
options: Use UUID= or LABEL= in the first field, not /dev/sdX or /dev/vdX
questions.explain: LVM paths like /dev/vg/lv are also stable; follow the wording of the task.

questions.q: Which command confirms autofs actually mounted remoteuser1's home over NFS?
questions.explain: The mount shows as nfs4 with the server:path source.

labs.title: Grow storage with a new disk
labs.scenario: Grow /exam to 900 MiB total. The VG does not have enough space, so add a new PV from a spare disk first. Keep the data.

labs.title: VFAT with label, at boot
labs.scenario: Create a 200 MiB VFAT filesystem labeled USBDATA and mount it at /mnt/usbdata at boot using LABEL=.
steps: parted -s /dev/vdb mkpart usb fat32 <start>MiB <start+200>MiB && udevadm settle

labs.title: Static NFS mount
labs.scenario: Mount node2:/shares/docs at /mnt/docs persistently, and check that it survives a reboot.

labs.title: autofs home directories from memory
labs.scenario: Without looking at earlier days, configure autofs so /rhome/remoteuser2 is mounted from node2:/rhome/remoteuser2 when remoteuser2 logs in.

title: Review: SELinux and the firewall
objective: Mixed exam-style practice on SELinux contexts, booleans, ports and firewalld.

questions.q: An exam task says "the web server must serve files from /srv/web in enforcing mode". Which two commands are essential?
questions.explain: The semanage rule survives a relabel; chcon does not.

questions.q: How do you find the correct file type to use for a service?
options: Look at the context of its default directory, e.g. `ls -Zd /var/www/html`, or its _selinux man page
questions.explain: Install selinux-policy-doc to get pages like `man httpd_selinux`.

questions.q: Show your local SELinux file-context customizations only.
questions.explain: -C lists only changes you made, which is handy for checking your work.

questions.q: The exam system is in permissive mode at the start. What should you do?
options: Set it to enforcing, now and in /etc/selinux/config, unless the task says otherwise
Leave it permissive to save time
Nothing; permissive is the same as enforcing
questions.explain: Tasks are graded with SELinux enforcing. Fix labels, don't turn SELinux off.

questions.q: You add a firewall rule with --permanent and forget to reload. Graders reboot the system. Is the rule active after the reboot?
options: Yes, permanent rules load at boot; but reload anyway so you can test now
questions.explain: A rule without --permanent is the one that disappears at reboot.

questions.q: Allow the httpd daemon to read user home directories through a persistent boolean.
questions.explain: Find booleans with `getsebool -a | grep httpd` or `semanage boolean -l | grep home`.

questions.q: Which command lists firewalld's rules for every zone at once?
questions.explain: --list-all shows only the default zone (or the one given with --zone).

questions.q: A service has the right file contexts and firewall, but still gets AVC denials for a network connection it makes. What is the likely fix?
options: Turn on the matching boolean, e.g. httpd_can_network_connect, with -P
questions.explain: Booleans switch optional behaviour in the policy on or off.

labs.title: Web content in a custom directory
labs.scenario: Serve /srv/web (containing index.html with "srv web") as Apache's DocumentRoot in enforcing mode, reachable from node2.
steps: vim /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf     # DocumentRoot "/srv/web" and <Directory "/srv/web"> Require all granted

labs.title: SELinux port and firewall together
labs.scenario: Make httpd listen on 8989 as well as 80. Fix SELinux and the firewall so both ports work from node2.

labs.title: Enforcing everywhere
labs.scenario: Set SELinux to permissive in both runtime and config (simulating a broken start state). Then fix it so it is enforcing now and after reboot.

labs.title: Firewall by zone
labs.scenario: Change the default zone to "home", make sure ssh and http are allowed in it permanently, and confirm the interface is in that zone.

title: Review: boot, targets and the bootloader
objective: Mixed exam-style practice on targets, root password reset and GRUB.

questions.q: The exam starts and you do not know node2's root password. What is expected?
options: Reset it by interrupting the boot (rd.break), usually as one of the tasks
questions.explain: Practise the reset until it takes under 4 minutes.

questions.q: After the root reset, the system reboots for a long time. Why?
options: SELinux is relabeling every file because of /.autorelabel
questions.explain: Let it finish. Don't power it off.

questions.q: Make the system boot into graphical.target by default.
questions.explain: Only if a desktop is installed; otherwise the target has nothing extra to start.

questions.q: Where do you add a kernel argument for one boot only?
options: At the GRUB menu: press e, edit the linux line, press Ctrl+X
questions.explain: The other methods are permanent.

questions.q: Add the argument crashkernel=256M to the default kernel only.
questions.explain: ALL means every kernel; DEFAULT means only the default one.

questions.q: What does `systemctl isolate rescue.target` do on a running system?
options: Stops most services and drops to single-user rescue mode
questions.explain: Do it from the console, not over SSH, because SSH stops.

questions.q: GRUB_TIMEOUT was changed in /etc/default/grub but the menu still waits 5 seconds. Why?
options: grub2-mkconfig was not run to regenerate grub.cfg
The file needs a reboot twice
GRUB_TIMEOUT must be in grub.cfg only
questions.explain: Run `grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg`.

questions.q: Which log shows what happened during the current boot?
questions.explain: `journalctl -b -1` shows the previous boot if the journal is persistent.

labs.title: Root password reset under time pressure
labs.scenario: Set a timer for 5 minutes. Reset node2's root password to "Exam@2026", with SELinux relabel, and log in.
verify: log in as root with Exam@2026

labs.title: Default target and GRUB timeout
labs.scenario: Make node2 boot into multi-user.target by default and set the GRUB menu timeout to 7 seconds. Reboot to confirm both.

labs.title: Kernel argument on the default kernel
labs.scenario: Add `nomodeset` to the default kernel only. Reboot and confirm, then remove it.

labs.title: Rescue mode repair
labs.scenario: Break sshd by adding an invalid line to /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-bad.conf, reboot into rescue.target from GRUB, find the error with journalctl and sshd -t, and fix it.
steps: # reboot, GRUB: e, add systemd.unit=rescue.target, Ctrl+X

title: Review: services, scheduling, logs, time and tuning
objective: Mixed exam-style practice on operating running systems.

questions.q: A task says "the service must start automatically at boot". Is `systemctl start` enough?
options: No; it must also be enabled, e.g. systemctl enable --now
questions.explain: Graders often reboot first and then test.

questions.q: Which cron line runs a job at 23:50 on the 1st and 15th of every month?
questions.explain: Lists use commas and ranges use a dash.

questions.q: Show the date and time chrony last synchronized, and how far off the clock is.
questions.explain: "System time" shows the current offset.

questions.q: The journal must survive reboots. Which step alone is enough when Storage=auto?
questions.explain: Setting Storage=persistent works too. Pick one and verify with --list-boots after a reboot.

questions.q: Kill the process with the highest CPU usage, given its PID is 4242, gracefully first.
questions.explain: Only use -9 if it does not exit after SIGTERM.

questions.q: Which command shows the reason a service failed to start?
options: systemctl status name, then journalctl -u name
questions.explain: status shows the last log lines; journalctl -u shows the whole history.

questions.q: Schedule `/usr/local/bin/cleanup.sh` for user harry every Monday at 07:15 as a cron job, without an editor.
questions.explain: `crontab -u harry -` reads the whole crontab from stdin. The first form keeps harry's existing jobs.

questions.q: A task says "set the tuning profile recommended by the system". What must also be true for it to persist?
options: The tuned service is enabled at boot
questions.explain: `systemctl enable --now tuned` then `tuned-adm profile $(tuned-adm recommend)`.

labs.title: Service health check
labs.scenario: Make sure httpd, chronyd, sshd and crond are all running and enabled. Find any failed unit on the system and fix it or reset its state.
steps: systemctl enable --now httpd chronyd sshd crond
verify: systemctl is-enabled httpd chronyd sshd crond; systemctl is-active httpd chronyd sshd crond

labs.title: Scheduling three ways
labs.scenario: For user natasha: a cron job that writes the date to /tmp/natasha-cron every 5 minutes. As root: an at job that writes "done" to /tmp/at-done in 3 minutes. And a systemd timer that runs `logger "timer tick"` every 15 minutes.
verify: crontab -l -u natasha; atq; systemctl list-timers tick.timer

labs.title: Logs and journal
labs.scenario: Make the journal persistent, then write a log line with priority local7.warning and find it both in /var/log/messages and in the journal.

labs.title: Time and tuning together
labs.scenario: Configure chrony to use node2 (or a server you choose) and set the time zone to Asia/Kolkata. Apply the recommended tuned profile. Verify all three.
steps: systemctl enable --now tuned && tuned-adm profile $(tuned-adm recommend)

title: Review: networking and software
objective: Mixed exam-style practice on IPv4, IPv6, hostnames, repositories and Flatpak.

questions.q: The exam gives you IP, netmask, gateway, DNS and hostname for node1. Where do you usually do this task?
options: On the console first, since SSH may drop when the address changes
questions.explain: After it works, you can use SSH for the rest.

questions.q: What is a netmask of 255.255.255.0 in prefix notation?
questions.explain: nmcli wants the prefix form: 192.168.1.10/24.

questions.q: Set the hostname to server1.example.com permanently.
questions.explain: Check with `hostnamectl`.

questions.q: Which nmcli property stops a profile from using DNS servers from DHCP?
questions.explain: Useful when a task gives you a fixed DNS server.

questions.q: Add a second DNS server 8.8.8.8 to the connection "eth0" without removing the existing one.
questions.explain: The `+` prefix appends to a list property; `-` removes an item.

questions.q: The repo task gives only a URL. Which lines do you write in the .repo file at minimum?
options: [id], name=, baseurl=URL, enabled=1, gpgcheck=0 (or 1 with the key the task gives)
questions.explain: Then run `dnf repolist` and install a package to prove it works.

questions.q: Install the package from the local file /root/tree-2.1.0.rpm, resolving dependencies from the repos.
questions.explain: Check with `rpm -q tree`.

questions.q: Which command lists the apps a Flatpak remote offers?
questions.explain: `flatpak list` shows only what is installed.

nmcli con mod "<profile>" ipv6.addresses fd00:10::11/64 ipv6.method manual

labs.scenario: Make node1 resolve node2 by name through /etc/hosts, and make sure the files are checked before DNS. Test both names.

title: Review: shell scripts
objective: Mixed exam-style practice on script inputs, conditions, loops and command output.

questions.q: A script must print an error and stop when no argument is given. Which test fits?
options: if [ $# -eq 0 ]; then echo "Usage: $0 arg" >&2; exit 1; fi
questions.explain: Send usage messages to stderr with >&2 and exit with a non-zero code.

questions.q: What does `for f in /etc/*.conf; do echo $f; done` loop over?
questions.explain: The shell expands the glob before the loop runs.

questions.q: Inside a script, save today's date in YYYY-MM-DD format into the variable today.
questions.explain: Use it like `tar -czf /root/backup-$today.tar.gz /etc`.

questions.q: A script is in /usr/local/bin with mode 644. Running `myscript` gives "Permission denied". Why?
options: It is not executable; run chmod +x (e.g. 755)
questions.explain: Without the x bit, the shell cannot run it by name.

questions.q: Loop over the lines of /root/hosts.txt (one host name per line) and ping each once.
accept: while read h; do ping -c 1 $h; done < /root/hosts.txt
for h in $(cat /root/hosts.txt); do ping -c 1 $h; done
while read h; do ping -c 1 "$h"; done < /root/hosts.txt
questions.explain: The while-read form also handles lines with spaces correctly.

questions.q: What does `$(( 5 + 3 ))` produce?
questions.explain: Bash arithmetic uses $(( )). Only whole numbers.

questions.q: What does `2>/dev/null` inside a script do for `find / -name x 2>/dev/null`?
options: Hides error messages so only real results reach the output
Saves errors to a file named null
questions.explain: The results still go to stdout, which you can redirect separately.

questions.q: How do you check inside a script that a user exists before creating it?
questions.explain: id exits 0 if the user exists, 1 if not.

title: Exam day strategy
objective: How to work through a full practical exam and not lose marks.

questions.q: What should you do in the first few minutes of the exam?
options: Read every task on both nodes, then start with networking, repos and the root reset
Start the storage tasks right away
Write notes about each task on paper for 30 minutes
questions.explain: Networking and repos are needed by many later tasks.

questions.q: What is the pass mark for EX200?
questions.explain: Tasks are graded by what works after a reboot, not by the commands you typed.

questions.q: Why reboot both nodes before the end of the exam?
options: To prove every change persists and to catch a broken fstab while you can still fix it
The exam requires it to submit
questions.explain: Leave at least 15 minutes for the final reboot and fixes.

questions.q: A task is taking too long. What is the best move?
options: Move on and come back later; every task is worth points
Keep going until it is solved
Skip the rest of the exam
questions.explain: One stuck task should not cost you three easy ones.

questions.q: Which change is the most dangerous to leave untested before a reboot?
questions.explain: Test every fstab change with `systemctl daemon-reload && mount -a` right away.

questions.q: The task says "user sarah must not have access to an interactive shell". Which check proves it?
options: grep sarah /etc/passwd shows /sbin/nologin as the shell
questions.explain: Verify every task with a command, not by memory.

questions.q: What should the SELinux mode be at the end of the exam?
options: Enforcing, unless a task explicitly says otherwise
questions.explain: Fix contexts, ports and booleans instead.

questions.q: Which is a good habit for every task?
options: Do it, verify it with a command, and note it as done
Do all tasks, then verify at the end only
Never verify; there is no time
questions.explain: Short verify commands take seconds and catch typos.

labs.title: Exam-day checklist run
labs.scenario: Take one full practice exam from the Exams tab with the timer on. At the end, reboot both nodes and use each task's verify commands to score yourself honestly.
steps: # Exams tab, pick an exam, press Start
# work node2 first if it needs a root reset, then networking and repos
# reboot both nodes at the 2 h 30 min mark and verify everything

labs.title: Build your own verify script
labs.scenario: Write /root/verify.sh that prints PASS or FAIL for five checks of your choice (e.g. hostname, SELinux enforcing, a mount, a user, a firewall service). Run it after a reboot.
steps: # check() { if eval "$2" &>/dev/null; then echo "PASS $1"; else echo "FAIL $1"; fi; }

labs.title: Speed round
labs.scenario: From a fresh snapshot, and within 30 minutes: set the network and hostname, configure the repos, create two users and a group, make an SGID directory, create an LV and mount it at boot, and set the recommended tuned profile.
steps: # use the earlier days' solutions only if you get stuck
